dailyBrief.text: Good morning, Smileys — and an extra hour of morning, since the clocks fell back overnight. It's a cloudy, mild Sunday in Solon, high near 68°, and the overnight sports split the house: the Cavs rolled 136–111 in Milwaukee behind Mobley and Allen, while Ohio State fell 30–18 at USC with freshman Luke Fahey starting for the injured Julian Sayin. Overseas, Iran claimed tankers hit mines in the Strait of Hormuz — a story Washington calls false and Iran's own Guards deny — with oil holding near $117. Today is stacked: the Browns play at Pittsburgh at 1 PM for first place in the AFC North, and it is the final day of early voting, 1 to 5 PM at the Cuyahoga County Board of Elections, before Tuesday's midterms. And the biggest story of all is still your own — after last night's trip to the hospital, everyone here is thinking of Kelly and the baby.

weekBrief.text: The week ahead in Solon starts mild and turns wet: cloudy and about 63° Monday, the warmest day of the week Tuesday at about 73° for Election Day, then showers build Wednesday, rain is likely Thursday, and a sharp cooldown drops Friday into the low 50s. Election week frames everything — early voting ends today at 5 PM, polls are open Tuesday 6:30 AM to 7:30 PM (66 Cuyahoga precincts have moved, so check yours), and the governor's and Senate races top a long ballot. In sports, the Browns play at Pittsburgh today for first place, the Cavs — fresh off a 136–111 rout in Milwaukee — host Oklahoma City Monday night, and Ohio State looks to regroup after Saturday's loss at USC. The standout deal remains Giant Eagle's BOGO-free sirloin tip roasts through Wednesday — and at home, with Kelly's labor starting last night, this is the week the Smiley family very likely grows by one.

items.title: Cavs vs Oklahoma City Thunder
Iran says tankers hit mines in the Strait of Hormuz — Washington calls it a lie to scare shipping
items.summary:
Iran told the International Maritime Organization that four tankers were damaged by naval mines in the Strait of Hormuz between October 27 and 30, and warned that the waterway is unsafe for commercial shipping. Tehran also raised its estimate of damage from the wider war to about $300 billion and repeated its demand for compensation.

The United States flatly rejected the claim. U.S. Central Command said its forces had cleared the strait's main transit lanes, that commercial ships are moving through them safely, and that Iran's mine story is false. American officials say the pattern fits a familiar playbook: raise the perceived risk of the route, push up insurance costs and oil prices, and gain leverage without firing a shot.

The stakes are global because the strait normally carries roughly a fifth of the world's oil and gas, and traffic is already down to a trickle after months of war. Every disputed incident moves energy prices — Brent crude closed Friday near $117 a barrel — and raises the chance of a miscalculation between navies operating in the same narrow water.

Watch for any independent confirmation from shipping firms or insurers, and for whether tanker traffic through the cleared lanes holds up in the coming days.

items.title: Iran's Revolutionary Guards say there are no mines in the strait — and blame the U.S. for the scare
items.summary:
In a statement carried by regional media, Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps denied that any mines have been laid in the Strait of Hormuz and accused Washington of inventing the story. The Guards pointed to the U.S. Navy's own mine-clearing operation as evidence the main shipping lanes are open, and said American statements are meant to create panic in energy markets.

The denial puts Iran's own institutions in public disagreement: the mine warning sent to the International Maritime Organization came through official Iranian channels, while the Guards — who control much of Iran's activity in the strait — now say the opposite. Outside analysts read the split as messaging aimed at different audiences, one for diplomats and insurers, another for domestic and military ones.

For shipping companies, the practical question has not changed: traffic through the strait remains a small fraction of normal, war-risk insurance is expensive, and no one wants to be the first owner to test the lanes at scale.

Watch which Iranian voice prevails in the next official statement — and whether any major shipping line publicly resumes regular transits.

items.title: U.S. approves a $2.1 billion Patriot missile sale to Ukraine — but the missiles are years away
items.summary:
The U.S. State Department has approved selling Ukraine roughly 600 Patriot PAC-3 interceptor missiles in a package Kyiv's officials value at about $2.1 billion, though some published totals run higher depending on what support is counted. Ukraine has been asking for more of the interceptors for months, calling them the only reliable defense against Russian ballistic missiles aimed at its cities and power grid.

The catch is timing. The missiles would be newly built rather than pulled from existing U.S. stockpiles, and President Volodymyr Zelensky has warned deliveries could take years — far too late for this winter's expected Russian strike campaign. Ukraine's partners, including Canada, Germany and Norway, are expected to help pay through allied funding programs, and Congress now gets its review period.

The approval is still a significant long-term commitment: it locks Ukraine into the Patriot ecosystem and signals that Western air-defense support is being planned in years, not news cycles, even as Kyiv presses for faster help from stockpiles that already exist.

Watch the congressional review, and whether any ally releases interceptors from its own inventory to bridge the gap this winter.

items.title: Congo's Ebola outbreak passes 5,000 deaths and spreads across three more borders
items.summary:
The Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo has now killed 5,026 people out of 10,351 confirmed cases, according to government figures released this week — a fatality rate near 49 percent. Declared in May, it is Congo's deadliest outbreak on record and the second-largest Ebola epidemic ever, behind only West Africa's 2014–2016 disaster.

The outbreak is driven by the rare Bundibugyo strain, for which there are no approved vaccines or treatments, and it is concentrated in the eastern provinces of Ituri and North Kivu, where conflict and weak infrastructure have hampered contact tracing. Officials estimate most new infections are appearing outside the contact chains they are monitoring, and many deaths are happening outside treatment centers.

It is no longer only Congo's emergency. Cases have been confirmed in Uganda, Kenya and South Sudan, Saudi Arabia has suspended travel links with Kenya, and the U.S. CDC has announced a 21-day monitoring policy for travelers arriving from Congo starting November 3.

Watch whether international funding and tracing staff surge in the next week — responders say that, more than anything, decides whether this keeps growing.

items.title: A third U.S. aircraft carrier heads for the Middle East as the Iran war grinds on
items.summary:
The United States is sending a third aircraft carrier to the Middle East, adding naval air power as the war with Iran stretches through its ninth month. The deployment comes while the two sides trade accusations over mines and shipping safety in the Strait of Hormuz, the conflict's central front.

The buildup sits alongside a diplomatic track that keeps stalling, and alongside other pressure signals, including the recent departure of non-emergency U.S. government staff from Saudi Arabia. President Trump has publicly suggested the conflict will be wrapped up soon, but the force posture tells a more open-ended story.

Three carrier groups in one theater is both deterrence and risk: it gives Washington options for a major operation, and it puts more ships and aircraft in crowded waters where a single incident could widen the war quickly — one reason oil markets are holding Brent near $117 a barrel.

Watch whether the carrier's arrival lines up with a negotiating breakthrough or with renewed strikes.

items.title: Qatar's talks to restart U.S.–Iran negotiations stall amid threats from both sides
items.summary:
Qatar's effort to restart direct negotiations between the United States and Iran has stalled, according to regional reporting, after days of mediated contacts that officials had earlier described as showing positive progress. The freeze leaves the two countries without a working diplomatic channel while their militaries face off over the Strait of Hormuz.

The sticking points are the same ones that have sunk previous rounds: Iran's nuclear program and stockpile of enriched uranium, the safety and control of shipping through the strait, and Tehran's demand for compensation for war damage, which it now puts at about $300 billion. Hard-line voices in both capitals have publicly threatened renewed strikes if talks fail.

Qatar has been the indispensable middleman in this conflict, and a stalled Doha channel matters because there is no obvious substitute. Previous openings have collapsed and later revived, so a pause is not necessarily an ending — but each week without talks is a week the military situation can drift.

Watch for any announcement of a new meeting date from Doha, Washington or Tehran; silence through the U.S. midterms would be its own signal.

items.title: The midterm campaign hits its final weekend with more than 50 million votes already cast
items.summary:
The fight for control of Congress is in its last weekend, and Americans have been voting early in record midterm numbers — more than 50 million ballots are already in, passing the roughly 46 million cast by this point in 2022. Republicans are defending narrow majorities in both chambers: 220 to 213 in the House and 53 to 47 in the Senate, with all 435 House seats and 35 Senate seats on Tuesday's ballot.

The weekend has brought a burst of legal and campaign fights, including a federal judge's order barring the Justice Department from threatening election officials over voter rolls, and President Trump restoring in-person rallies in Kansas and Iowa for Sunday after cancelling them earlier in the week. Polls favor Democrats to take the House, with a harder but plausible path to the Senate running through states like Alaska, Maine and Texas.

Confidence in the count itself remains broad: about 76 percent of voters say they trust their ballots will be counted accurately, even as litigation flies in several states. The combination of huge early turnout and close margins means Tuesday night could be long in the races that decide both chambers.

Watch Alaska's Senate race, the late legal fights over ballot eligibility, and whether Election Day turnout matches the early-vote surge.

items.title: Judge orders the Justice Department to stop threatening election officials over voter rolls
items.summary:
A federal judge has issued a temporary restraining order barring the Trump administration's Justice Department from threatening to prosecute state and local election officials who refuse its demands about alleged noncitizen voters. U.S. District Judge Trina Thompson found that, days before the election, the balance of equities and the public interest favored the officials running the vote on the ground.

The order stops the department from demanding that local officials pull voters from statewide rolls, refuse ballots to specific voters, or set ballots aside in the midterms based on the administration's lists. It follows an appeals court decision again refusing to let the administration set aside roughly 20,000 California mail ballots it says may belong to noncitizens — the government's second loss in that case this week.

The administration frames its election push as security and confidence-building. Election officials from both parties, and now several judges, call it federal overreach into elections the Constitution leaves to the states.

The restraining order runs through November 14; watch for an administration appeal and for how states handle any further federal demands before Tuesday.

items.title: Trump's approval is net-positive in just eight states heading into Tuesday's vote
items.summary:
President Trump's job approval is underwater in 42 of 50 states days before the midterms, according to Civiqs' state-by-state tracking. He is net-positive only in Alabama, Arkansas, Idaho, North Dakota, Oklahoma, Utah, West Virginia and Wyoming — deep-red states he has carried repeatedly — with Wyoming his strongest at about plus-14 and Kansas exactly even.

The numbers that worry Republicans are in the battlegrounds: every swing state with a tight Senate race is well underwater, including Ohio at about minus-18, Michigan at minus-26, Maine at minus-29, Alaska at minus-25 and Texas at minus-20. A new Emerson College poll puts Trump's national approval at 37 percent, the lowest of his second term in that survey, alongside a double-digit Democratic lead on the generic congressional ballot.

A president's approval is historically the single best predictor of midterm losses, which is why these figures have Republicans bracing. Most voters have already decided or already voted, so the remaining question is whether late turnout can bend the pattern.

Watch Tuesday's results in the underwater swing states — they will test whether approval polling still predicts midterm outcomes in an era of massive early voting.

items.title: Maine's Senate race is the most expensive per person in America — about $160 for every resident
items.summary:
The Maine Senate race between five-term Republican Sen. Susan Collins and Democrat Troy Jackson, the former state Senate president, has drawn roughly $218 million in broadcast advertising — about $160 for every person in the state, the highest per-capita figure of any competitive Senate race, according to a USA Today analysis of AdImpact data. Nationally, Republicans are outspending Democrats by about $305 million across the competitive Senate races.

Collins is uniquely exposed: she is the only Republican running for re-election in a state Trump lost in 2024. Door-knockers say voters are talking less about the ads than about affordability — Maine has New England's lowest median income, and heating-oil costs are up sharply as winter approaches, a pocketbook fight both campaigns are trying to own.

Small states with cheap media markets are where record national money stretches furthest, which is why Maine, and Alaska at about $140 per person, top the per-capita chart far ahead of Texas at roughly $14.

Watch whether the spending gap shows up in Tuesday's margin — and whether Collins's personal brand can still outrun a bad national environment for her party.

items.title: Trump puts his Kansas and Iowa rallies back on for today after cancelling them
items.summary:
President Trump has restored in-person rallies in Kansas and Iowa for today, Sunday, two days before the midterms, after abruptly cancelling both earlier in the week, according to AFP reporting. The reversal returns the traditional closing-weekend swing through two states where Republicans are defending vulnerable Senate seats.

The schedule whiplash is the second in days: the president had shifted toward a 72-hour tele-rally format aimed at nearly 20 states, with Vice President JD Vance carrying much of the in-person load, including a recent rally in Youngstown, Ohio. Closing weekends are about base turnout rather than persuasion, and both parties are now flooding the same handful of states.

With more than 50 million votes already cast, today's rallies are aimed at the shrinking slice of supporters who still vote in person on Election Day itself.

Watch the size and energy of today's crowds — and whether any other cancelled stops quietly return to the schedule before Tuesday.

items.title: Wall Street's AI selloff: Nasdaq's worst day since June, and Intel lost nearly a third of its value
items.summary:
U.S. stocks closed sharply lower on Friday as investors bailed out of the artificial-intelligence trade. The Nasdaq Composite fell 2.86 percent to 25,437 — its biggest one-day drop since June 5 — while the S&P 500 lost 1.82 percent to about 7,580 and the Dow fell 1.09 percent to about 51,770. October became the technology sector's worst month since March 2025.

Intel was the epicenter, plunging 28.6 percent after a weak outlook tied to soft PC demand and shutdowns at its operations in Israel, erasing roughly $140 billion in market value in its worst session in decades. The selling spread across chips and hardware: AMD fell 10.9 percent, Nvidia 4.2 percent, the semiconductor index 7.2 percent, and server makers Dell and HP about 10 percent each. Crypto stocks slid with the Binance hack news, while energy, staples, utilities and health care sheltered.

Underneath the panic, earnings season itself is strong — about 82 percent of the S&P 500 companies that have reported beat estimates, with profits up roughly 31.6 percent. The argument on Wall Street is no longer whether AI works, but whether the hundreds of billions being spent on it will pay back fast enough to justify September's prices.

Markets are closed Sunday; watch Monday's open for whether Friday was capitulation or the start of a deeper repricing.

items.title: The $6.3 billion Binance hack: North Korea's TraderTraitor unit blamed for crypto's biggest theft
items.summary:
Attackers drained about $6.36 billion from Binance, the world's largest crypto exchange, on Thursday evening — most of it in roughly 20 minutes starting at 4:05 p.m. Eastern, across ten blockchains including Bitcoin, Ethereum, Solana and Tron. Blockchain intelligence firm TRM Labs, which tracked the flows, calls it the largest cryptocurrency theft on record, more than four times the $1.5 billion Bybit hack of February 2025.

TRM attributes the attack with high confidence to TraderTraitor, North Korea's elite state hacking unit — the same group the FBI blamed for Bybit — and other analytics firms have publicly agreed. Binance says the breach began with a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop that let attackers submit unauthorized withdrawals; it found no evidence that wallet private keys leaked. On Ethereum, the attackers used a delegation trick to turn a Binance hot wallet into a sweeper under their control, with pre-signed authorizations prepared in advance.

Binance and partners including Tether and Circle have frozen roughly $3 billion of the stolen assets. Customer deposits were never affected, withdrawals are paused and expected to resume shortly, and the exchange says its SAFU insurance fund will cover all losses. U.S. intelligence has long assessed that Pyongyang nets at least $1 billion a year from crypto theft to fund weapons programs — which makes a $6.3 billion haul a national-security story, not just a market one.

Watch the laundering trail: how much of the unfrozen half starts moving, and whether exchanges worldwide tighten withdrawal controls in response.

items.title: Oil closes near $117 a barrel as the Hormuz standoff starves the world's most important shipping lane
items.summary:
Brent crude closed Friday at about $117.40 a barrel, up 3.1 percent on the day and on course for a fourth straight monthly gain, while U.S. West Texas Intermediate settled near $106. The latest leg up came as Iran warned the International Maritime Organization that tankers had struck mines in the Strait of Hormuz — a claim the U.S. military calls false — and tanker traffic through the strait stayed at single digits per day, versus more than a hundred transits on a normal pre-war day.

The strait normally carries about a fifth of global oil and gas supply, so even a partial, months-long closure keeps a risk premium baked into every barrel. Traders are also pricing the possibility that the U.S. resumes major strikes after Tuesday's midterm elections, a scenario military sources have hinted at and the White House has publicly downplayed.

For households far from the Gulf, the transmission is direct: sustained $117 oil feeds into gasoline, diesel, heating oil and airfares with a lag of weeks, which is why Maine voters' heating bills and Ohio pump prices are part of the same story.

Watch Monday's Asian open and any change in actual tanker transits — prices will follow ships, not statements, once markets reopen.

items.title: The Bank of England warns the AI boom could become a financial-stability risk
items.summary:
The Bank of England has used a flagship speech on artificial intelligence and asset valuations to formally warn that the AI investment boom carries financial-stability risks. The Bank's Financial Policy Committee says stretched valuations in AI-linked stocks, combined with the scale of debt being raised to fund data centers, could amplify a market correction.

The warning landed the same week as Friday's selloff, in which the Nasdaq posted its worst day since June and Intel lost more than a quarter of its value in a session. British regulators are not predicting a crash; they are saying the plumbing matters — if AI spending is financed with borrowed money and the expected returns arrive late, losses can spread beyond shareholders to lenders.

Central banks move slowly and choose words carefully, so a public systemic-risk framing from Threadneedle Street is a marker of how seriously officials now take the concentration of global markets in a handful of AI names.

Watch whether the Federal Reserve echoes the language in its next financial-stability report, and whether credit spreads on data-center debt start to widen.

items.title: Intel's Israel AI campus sits idle as the Hormuz closure snarls its chip shipments
items.summary:
Intel has shut down operations at its Haifa AI campus in Israel, idling advanced chip work after the closure of the Strait of Hormuz choked the specialized shipping routes the site depends on, according to Reuters reporting. Finished and in-process chips have been stuck at the port of Haifa as carriers avoid the region.

The shutdown became one of the drivers of Intel's disastrous Friday: the stock fell 28.6 percent after a weak outlook that cited soft PC demand alongside the Israel disruption, erasing roughly $140 billion in market value. Intel is one of the largest private employers in Israel's tech sector, so an extended halt ripples through the local economy as well as the chip supply chain.

The episode is a concrete example of how a shipping crisis in one narrow strait reaches into products that never touch oil — advanced processors move by tightly scheduled, specialized logistics, and there is no quick substitute when a node goes dark.

Watch for Intel updates on restarting Haifa, and whether customers begin qualifying second sources for the affected chips.

items.title: Companies will spend $620 billion on AI this year — and plan to spend $200 billion more next year
items.summary:
Global corporate spending on artificial intelligence is on track to reach about $620 billion in 2026, according to new survey-based estimates, with companies already guiding toward roughly $200 billion in additional spending in 2027. The figures cover data centers, chips, software and the power infrastructure to run them.

Chief financial officers are split on what it buys. The survey work finds a clear divide between firms reporting measurable productivity gains — concentrated in customer support, coding and logistics — and a long tail still spending defensively because competitors are. That split is exactly what spooked equity markets on Friday, when Intel's outlook and broader AI doubts knocked 2.86 percent off the Nasdaq.

The spending wave is real economic activity regardless of the stock debate: it is driving construction, utility demand and chip orders across the U.S., including in Ohio's data-center corridor. The question investors are asking is about timing — returns in years versus bills due now.

Watch the next round of hyperscaler capital-spending guidance; any hint of a pause would test both markets and local construction pipelines.

items.title: The clocks fell back overnight — daylight saving time is over until March
items.summary:
Daylight saving time ended at 2 a.m. today, Sunday, November 1, when clocks across most of the United States moved back one hour to standard time. If you woke up feeling like you gained an hour, you did — sunrise and sunset both arrive an hour earlier by the clock until daylight saving returns on March 14, 2027. Arizona and Hawaii stay on standard time year-round and did not change.

The twice-yearly switch remains politically unsettled. Nineteen states have passed laws or resolutions favoring permanent daylight saving time, but Congress has not enacted the federal change those laws need, and the Sunshine Protection Act has stalled. Sleep researchers generally favor permanent standard time; retail and recreation industries favor permanent daylight time.

The practical advice is unglamorous and proven: AAA warns the first evenings of standard time bring a spike in drowsy-driving and pedestrian crashes as commutes suddenly happen in the dark. It is also the traditional weekend to test smoke and carbon-monoxide detectors and swap their batteries.

Watch Congress in the new session — a midterm reshuffle could revive, or bury, the permanent-time bills for another cycle.

items.title: Halloween tornadoes tore through central Oklahoma, injuring 14 — and remarkably, no one died
items.summary:
A rare Halloween severe-weather outbreak spawned at least three tornadoes across central Oklahoma on Saturday, including an EF2 that hit Shawnee, damaging more than 200 structures and injuring 14 people. The National Weather Service office in Norman confirmed tornadoes rated EF1 through EF2, with the strongest winds estimated around 120 mph in the Shawnee area; other damage was reported around Prague, Meeker and the Oklahoma City metro.

The Storm Prediction Center had flagged a Slight Risk for the region, and the tornadoes arrived during trick-or-treat hours — the nightmare scheduling for any fall outbreak. Emergency managers credited warnings and the fact that many families were already indoors or in groups with the outcome every responder hopes for: injuries, but zero fatalities.

Fall is Oklahoma's secondary severe season, when warm Gulf air collides with strengthening cold fronts — the same pattern that put northern Ohio under a windy, unsettled Halloween. Damage assessments continue today, and the weather service will finalize ratings for the remaining tracks.

Watch for the final survey results and for power-restoration timelines in Pottawatomie County, where the heaviest damage is concentrated.

items.title: A salmonella outbreak tied to recalled eggs has sickened 92 people in seven states
items.summary:
Federal health officials say 92 people have been sickened and 21 hospitalized in a salmonella outbreak linked to eggs from Black Sheep Egg Company, which has recalled eggs distributed since September 8. Illnesses are reported across California, Colorado, Texas, Arizona, Nevada, Oregon, Washington and Michigan, with California seeing the most cases.

The FDA's recall notice covers specified lots sold through distributors and retailers, and the CDC is urging households to check cartons against the published codes, throw out or return any matches, and clean surfaces the eggs touched. No deaths have been reported, and investigators are still working out how the contamination entered the supply chain.

Eggs are one of the most common salmonella vehicles, and outbreaks tied to shell eggs tend to surface slowly because cartons sit in refrigerators for weeks. Officials expect the case count to rise as state labs confirm pending samples.

Check your fridge against the FDA lot list — and watch for the recall to expand, as egg recalls often do in their second week.

items.title: Food assistance will go out only in part this month as the shutdown fight lands in court
items.summary:
November SNAP benefits — the food assistance that reaches about 42 million Americans — will be paid only partially, after two federal judges ordered the administration to use contingency funds rather than let the program lapse during the government shutdown. The contingency reserve holds roughly $5 to $6 billion against a program that costs about $8 billion a month, so states are preparing reduced or delayed payments.

About 25 states sued to force the payments, arguing the government had both the money and the legal duty to keep food aid flowing. The administration has directed states to issue what it can, but governors warn that reprogramming benefit systems mid-month will produce uneven results — some households paid late, some paid less, some paid twice by mistake and clawed back.

Food banks are bracing for the gap regardless of the court outcome, and GoFundMe says shutdown-related fundraisers have already raised more than $2.3 million for federal workers and affected families. For local pantries in Northeast Ohio, November is already the highest-demand month of the year.

Watch for Ohio's payment schedule announcement — the state has to tell recipients this week what November will actually look like.

items.title: Two killed in a foggy overnight pileup that closed I-90 in Erie County, Pennsylvania
items.summary:
Two people were killed and several others injured in a chain-reaction crash involving three semi-trucks and two passenger cars on Interstate 90 in Erie County, Pennsylvania, late Saturday night. Dense fog cut visibility to near zero at the time, and state police closed both directions of the interstate for hours while crews investigated and cleared the wreckage.

Detours routed traffic onto Route 20 and nearby state routes through the early morning, and officials urged drivers to avoid the corridor until the highway fully reopened. The names of those killed have not been released pending family notification.

Lake-effect season is when the I-90 corridor between Cleveland and Buffalo turns treacherous in two ways at once — fog off the still-warm lake now, snow squalls soon. It is the same stretch many Northeast Ohio families drive for Thanksgiving, which makes this weekend's crash a grim early-season warning.

Watch for the state police reconstruction report, and check conditions before any lake-corridor driving this month — visibility can go from clear to zero in a single mile.

items.title: Strangers have raised $2.3 million for shutdown-hit families on GoFundMe — and the requests keep coming
items.summary:
GoFundMe says more than $2.3 million has been raised across 800-plus verified fundraisers on its government-shutdown hub, as missed paychecks and partial food benefits push federal workers and military families to ask strangers for help. The company is distributing $500 grants to eligible campaigns and waiving its usual verification delays for shutdown-related fundraisers.

The campaigns cluster where federal employment does — Florida, Texas, Virginia, California and Maryland lead — and the asks are strikingly basic: rent, groceries, gas to get to unpaid shifts. Organizers say donations spike each time a pay date passes without a check, and again when the SNAP partial-payment news broke Saturday.

Crowdfunding is a poor substitute for a functioning budget process, and everyone involved says so — but it is also a real-time map of where the shutdown hurts first, drawn by the people living it.

Watch whether the hub's totals accelerate this week, when the next federal pay cycle and the reduced SNAP payments land at the same time.

items.title: Ohio State falls 30–18 at USC as freshman Fahey starts for the injured Sayin
items.summary:
No. 2 Ohio State lost 30–18 to USC at the Los Angeles Coliseum on Saturday night, playing without quarterback Julian Sayin, who is out indefinitely with an injury to his throwing arm. Freshman Luke Fahey started in his place and finished 21-of-38 for 260 yards and one touchdown.

The Buckeyes hurt themselves as much as USC did: 11 penalties for 75 yards stalled drive after drive, and Ohio State settled for four field goals before finally scoring its lone touchdown. USC's defense, meanwhile, made the young quarterback play from behind for most of the second half.

Ohio State entered the night 6–1, so the loss does not end its College Football Playoff hopes — but it removes the margin for error. How the Buckeyes respond, and how long Sayin is actually out, now define their November.

Watch for the first official update on Sayin's timeline this week; everything about Ohio State's ceiling runs through his throwing arm.

items.title: Cavs rout the Bucks 136–111 in Milwaukee for their first road win of the season
items.summary:
The Cavaliers blew out the Bucks 136–111 at Fiserv Forum on Saturday night, riding a 48–21 second quarter to a 72–46 halftime lead and never looking back. Evan Mobley led Cleveland with 27 points, Jarrett Allen added 25 points and 11 rebounds, Donovan Mitchell scored 15 and James Harden 13.

It was Cleveland's first road win of the season and it came on the second night of a back-to-back, a night after beating Toronto at home. The Cavs' frontcourt set the tone early — Mobley and Allen overwhelmed Milwaukee inside while the Bucks' defense never found an answer for Cleveland's pace.

At 4–2, the Cavs have steadied themselves after a choppy opening week, and a rout this complete, on the road, on tired legs, is the kind of early-season result that suggests the rotation is settling.

Next up: Oklahoma City visits Rocket Arena tomorrow night, Monday, at 7 p.m. on Peacock/NBCSN — a sterner test against one of the West's best, even with the Thunder banged up.

items.title: DeWine expects 40–45% midterm turnout as Vance stumps for Ohio Republicans in Youngstown
items.summary:
Gov. Mike DeWine is predicting Ohio midterm turnout of 40 to 45 percent of registered voters, slightly below the 2022 midterms, as Vice President JD Vance headlined a get-out-the-vote rally in Youngstown this weekend for the Republican ticket. Ohio's ballot is topped by the race to succeed DeWine, the closely watched Senate contest, and every statewide executive office.

Early-voting numbers support a big number: Cuyahoga County alone passed 140,000 early ballots on Saturday, ahead of its 2022 pace, and statewide figures point the same direction. Vance's Youngstown stop targeted the Mahoning Valley's working-class voters, whose shift over the past decade has remade Ohio politics.

Ohio no longer sits at the center of the national Senate map the way it once did, but its results will still be read as a referendum on the administration — the president's approval in Ohio sits at about minus-18 in the latest state tracking, which is why both parties are spending the final weekend here.

Final early voting runs today, Sunday, from 1 to 5 p.m. at the Cuyahoga County Board of Elections; after that, the only way to vote is at your precinct on Tuesday between 6:30 a.m. and 7:30 p.m.

items.title: Today is the last day to vote early in Cuyahoga County — 1 to 5 p.m., and 66 precincts have moved
items.summary:
Cuyahoga County's early in-person voting ends today, Sunday, November 1, with a single session from 1:00 to 5:00 p.m. at the Board of Elections, 1803 Superior Avenue in Cleveland. More than 140,000 county residents have already voted early ahead of Tuesday's midterms, and officials expect today's final session to be brisk.

Two practical warnings come with the deadline. First, there is no early voting tomorrow, Monday — after 5 p.m. today, the only remaining option is your assigned precinct on Election Day, Tuesday, from 6:30 a.m. to 7:30 p.m. Second, 66 Cuyahoga County precincts have new polling locations this cycle, so even habitual Election Day voters should look up their location before Tuesday morning rather than driving on muscle memory.

Solon voters vote at the county's early center today or at their Solon precincts on Tuesday; bring a photo ID, and remember that Ohio's contested races this year include governor, U.S. Senate and every statewide office.

Check your registration and polling place at the Board of Elections site before you go — five minutes today beats a wrong line on Tuesday.

items.title: Cleveland Metroparks unveils $15 million in Emerald Necklace upgrades for its centennial
items.summary:
Cleveland Metroparks has announced $15 million in trail and facility improvements across the Emerald Necklace as the park district approaches its centennial in 2027. The plan covers trail resurfacing, bridge work and trailhead upgrades spread across the system's 25,000 acres and more than 100 miles of trails.

The Emerald Necklace — the ring of reservations that arcs around Cuyahoga County, including the South Chagrin Reservation in Solon — is one of the oldest and most-visited metropolitan park systems in the country. Park officials framed the investment as catching up on a decade of heavy use: trails are the system's most-used feature, and deferred maintenance has been building since the pandemic surge in outdoor recreation.

For Solon families, the South Chagrin Reservation is the local front door to the system — its trails along the Chagrin River, including the path toward Squaw Rock, are among the most walked in the county. Which specific segments get resurfaced first will matter to anyone with a regular loop.

Watch for the phased construction schedule this winter; work is expected to start in spring 2027, timed to the centennial year.

items.title: Cuyahoga County says it cut its criminal-case backlog 30% — judges credit new scheduling rules
items.summary:
Cuyahoga County judges say new scheduling and case-management practices have cut the court's criminal backlog by about 30 percent, according to Signal Cleveland's reporting on the court's post-pandemic caseload. The backlog ballooned during COVID-era shutdowns and staffing shortages and has been one of the county justice system's defining problems since.

A smaller backlog is not an abstraction: it means defendants waiting in jail for trial get hearings sooner, victims and witnesses are not asked to stay ready for years, and prosecutors and public defenders can work cases while evidence and memories are fresh. Court administrators credit firmer trial dates, earlier discovery deadlines and dedicated docket time for the oldest cases.

The court still carries more pending cases than it did before the pandemic, and judges caution that staffing — bailiffs, court reporters, public defenders — remains the binding constraint. But the direction, for the first time in years, is clearly down.

Watch the year-end caseload report; if the trend holds through the holidays, the court could enter 2027 below its pre-pandemic average case age.

baby.tip: For the first hours after birth, skin-to-skin contact is the main event: baby on a parent's chest helps regulate the baby's temperature, breathing and blood sugar, and it is something Mike can do too, not just Kelly. Keep the hospital bag's long phone charger within reach, drink water whenever it's offered, and let the nurses set the pace — resting while the baby rests starts now, not at home.
baby.fact: A newborn's stomach is tiny — about the size of a cherry on day one, holding roughly a teaspoon or two at a time. That is why brand-new babies feed so often, and why frequent small feeds in the first days are exactly right rather than a sign something is wrong.
baby.fun: Today's tiny prep mission, hospital edition: start the notes-app list neither of you will remember later — first song played for the baby, the weather outside (cloudy and in the upper 60s in Solon), and one line about how each of you is feeling. Future you will be very glad past you bothered.
